title: Astika stops the fire
hook: a young sage, half from the snakes' own family, asks the king for one gift: stop the fire
carry: listening to the sacred story is itself devotion
tomorrow: what did a king in heaven do to get sent back down?

segments.voice: Yesterday: a dead snake on a silent sage, a son's curse, and Takshaka hidden in a fruit. Karma is a chain; kshama can break it.
screen: `KARMA IS A CHAIN; KSHAMA CAN BREAK IT.`

segments.voice: The fire is lit. Janamejaya has heard how his father died, and his priests begin the snake sacrifice. As they chant, snakes are drawn from everywhere into the flames, the text says, great and small, crying out as they fall. Takshaka, the one the king most wants, has fled to Indra for protection. And a young man is walking toward the sacrifice, sent by his mother. His name is Astika. His father is a sage, his mother is the sister of a snake king, and he has come to stop the fire.
screen: `THE FIRE IS LIT.` → `TAKSHAKA HIDES WITH INDRA.` → `A YOUNG SAGE IS COMING.`

segments.voice: Astika's story starts with his father, a sage named Jaratkaru, who wanted no wife and no home. One day he found his ancestors hanging head down over a pit, holding a thin root that a rat was gnawing. They were falling, they told him, because their line would end with him. So Jaratkaru agreed to marry, on strange terms: only a bride who shared his name. The snake king Vasuki had a sister named Jaratkaru, and he'd been told a child of this marriage would save the snakes. That child is Astika. At the sacrifice, Astika doesn't argue or threaten. He praises the king, the priests and the fire, so well that Janamejaya wants to give him a gift. Ask for anything, the king says. And Astika asks: stop the sacrifice. The king offers other gifts. Astika holds to his one request. By now Takshaka is falling toward the flames, held in the air above them. The assembly urges the king to keep his word, and Janamejaya does. The fire stops. Takshaka is spared. And at this sacrifice, the text says, Vaishampayana tells the king his family's great story. So the frame closes on a king who came to burn and stayed to listen. Hindus call that shravana, hearing, and the Bhagavata Purana names it first among the ways of devotion. That's why families still gather for katha, a sacred story told aloud over many evenings, and why the Mahabharata itself promises good to those who hear it. On the first day of this year we met him beside a fire. We leave him listening.
screen: `A SAGE WHO WANTED NO WIFE.` · `A BRIDE WHO SHARED HIS NAME.` · `PRAISE, THEN ONE REQUEST.` · `THE KING KEEPS HIS WORD.` · then, large: `LISTENING TO THE SACRED STORY IS ITSELF DEVOTION.`

segments.voice: For two minutes, just listen, without planning what you'll say back: to someone at home telling you about their day, to a recorded bhajan or chant, or to a few lines of a sacred text read aloud. When your mind starts drafting a reply, set it down and go back to hearing. Janamejaya came to burn, and stayed to listen.
Adi Parva. The opening book, where Astika's request ends the snake sacrifice, and the great story begins.
Hold on to this: listening to the sacred story is itself devotion. Tomorrow: what did a king in heaven do to get sent back down? See you then.

screen: `DAY 703 COUNTS.` → `THE MAHABHARATA · 7 OF 182.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT DID A KING IN HEAVEN DO TO GET SENT BACK DOWN?`

howItsDone: Many Hindu families and temples hold katha: a sacred story, such as the Mahabharata, the Ramayana or the Bhagavata Purana, told or recited aloud, sometimes over many evenings, and hearing it is held to be devotion in itself. In some households Astika's name is remembered as a protection against snakes, in keeping with the promise the story records.

Astika.meaning: the young sage, Vasuki's nephew, who asks for the fire to stop

Jaratkaru.meaning: Astika's father, a sage, and also his mother's name

Vasuki.meaning: a snake king, Kadru's son and Astika's uncle

Vaishampayana.meaning: Vyasa's disciple, who tells Janamejaya his ancestors' story

shravana.meaning: hearing: listening to sacred story as devotion

katha.meaning: a sacred story told or recited aloud

Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Adivansavatarana Parva (Vaishampayana begins the Kuru story)
Bhagavata Purana, Book 7 (Prahlada names hearing, shravana, first among the forms of devotion)
